Nat arrives first, then the boys, Sundays, stepping stones, and patty pans, with Naughty Nan and a firebrand or two. Alcott writes with humor and tenderness about a school where kindness is the curriculum. The book endures as a classic of childhood, and of Jo March grown into a teacher.
27901-jewish-literature-and-other-essays:
Gustav Karpeles published Jewish Literature and Other Essays in Philadelphia in 1895 with the Jewish Publication Society of America. The essays survey the Talmud, women in Jewish literature, Moses Maimonides, Jewish troubadours, humor and love in Jewish poetry, and the Jewish stage.

Karpeles opens by rebuking Heine for condemning Jewish women ignorant of their poetry's golden age, noting that popular knowledge of the field was only fifty years old. The book remains a readable nineteenth-century guide to a literature Karpeles compares to a Hebrew Pompeii newly unearthed. Later essays treat the Jew's quest in Africa, a Jewish king in Poland, Leopold Zunz, and Heinrich Heine.
2821-the-story-of-the-gadsbys:
Rudyard Kipling wrote this story of the Gadsbys as an awful warning, addressing Captain J. Mafflin of the Duke of Derry's Hussars in the preface. Poor Dear Mamma, The World Without, and The Tents of Kedar follow a young officer's courtship and marriage.

With Any Amazement, The Garden of Eden, and Fatima carry the tale through love, army life, and disillusion in India. Kipling writes in scenes and dialogue, with wit and bite. The book offers a sharp, early portrait of Anglo Indian society, and of a marriage under strain.
29130-billy-topsail-company-a-story-for-:
Norman Duncan wrote this 1910 boys' story, Billy Topsail and Company, published by Fleming H. Revell in New York, Chicago, Toronto, London, and Edinburgh. The book continues The Adventures of Billy Topsail, which the Brooklyn Eagle praised for portraying actual Newfoundland life without invention. Every boy who knows Billy, the publisher says, will welcome this continuation among the hardy sons of the sea.

A frontispiece shows Bill o' Burnt Bay and the boys of the Spot Cash unable to fathom the mystery of the Black Eagle. Duncan, author of Doctor Luke of the Labrador, writes clean, pure, and stimulating adventure, true to life. Readers get a stirring Newfoundland sea story for boys, full of boats, boys, and the northern coast.
2920-four-short-plays:
John Galsworthy collected four short plays under the heading Hall-Marked and Others, drawn from his Six Short Plays. Hall-Marked, a satiric trifle, opens in a bungalow sitting room with French windows, where a dripping woman runs in carrying a wet Scotch terrier. Defeat, The Sun, and Punch and Go complete the set, each running a single sharp situation.

The plays show Galsworthy's range in miniature, from society comedy to wartime feeling. One later scene has a young officer refuse a girl's kiss, then bend to her forehead, only for her to press her mouth to his and cling. The collection suits readers who want Galsworthy in brief, where a whole social world fits inside one room and one evening.
2940-evolution-and-ethics-and-other-essa:
Thomas Henry Huxley collected Evolution and Ethics and Other Essays around his Romanes Lecture at Oxford, the second in the series founded by George Romanes. Huxley mourns Romanes, dead in the flower of his age, a friend valued for kindly nature and zeal for knowledge. He recalls receiving Romanes's early work as a secretary of the Royal Society and rejoicing at the accession to the little army of workers in science. The essays restate the patent facts of variation.

Domestic plants and animals vary widely under favorable conditions, and interbreeding can fix a variety into a race that comes true from seed. Such races may differ as widely as admitted species. The book asks how ethics can stand against a natural process that favors self-assertion, and it remains Huxley's most philosophical work.
29420-american-rural-highways:
Issued in the Agricultural Engineering Series under consulting editor E. B. McCormick, this manual treats the purpose and utility of rural highways in America. A preface dated at Ames, Iowa, in August 1920 frames the transport problem as national in scope, and chapters work from first principles toward practice. The book speaks to engineers, farmers, and county officials building roads for a motor age.

Its pages cover road purpose, design, and use, with the technical care of a college text, including notes on grades, loads, and surfaces. The aim is practical: better farm-to-market roads for a growing nation. Historians of transport and rural America will find a detailed record of how highway science was taught just as cars remade the countryside.
29444-the-machinery-of-the-universe-mech:
A. E. Dolbear, professor of physics and astronomy at Tufts College, wrote this 1897 book in the Romance of Science series, printed by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London and E. and J. B. Young in New York. Dolbear sets out mechanical conceptions of physical phenomena: how energy, motion, and forces might be pictured as machinery of the universe, from imponderables to transformations of light and electricity.

Chapters trace antecedents of electricity, the nature of what is transformed, and the series of changes that yield light, with positive and negative electricity weighed in turn. The prose is that of a teacher speaking to general readers. Students of Victorian science will find a clear window on how physicists pictured nature just before the electron age.
29515-the-battle-of-the-bays:
Owen Seaman's 1902 book of verse, printed by John Lane at the Bodley Head in London and New York, takes its title from its opening sequence, The Battle of the Bays. Its poems include a song of renunciation, verses for the albums of crowned heads only, Marsyas in Hades, the rhyme of the kipperling, a ballad of a bun, and a Vigo-Street eclogue. An ode to spring in the metropolis follows.

Seaman, known also for In Cap and Bells and Horace at Cambridge, writes light verse with a sharp, classical edge. His battle of the bays is a witty contest of poets, fought with rhyme. Readers of Edwardian light verse will find a clever, polished collection, funny and learned at once.
30007-a-dear-little-girl-s-thanksgiving-:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote A Dear Little Girl's Thanksgiving Holidays, part of the Dear Little Girl series, printed by the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin. The copyright, held by George W. Jacobs and Company, is dated 1912, and this printing is dated 1924. Edna comes home from school one Friday afternoon to find a letter from grandma, with no real news but an invitation of the Thanksgiving kind.

Grandma wants the whole family for an old-fashioned Thanksgiving, like those of her youth, since she and grandpa grow old and may not gather them all again. Edna and her mother plan to go a day or two ahead, while Celia, the boys, and father follow, father not free until Wednesday afternoon. Twelve chapters follow: the invitation, Reliance, a missing key, a hearty dinner, the red book, the old house, the mill stream, Jetty's party, and farewells.
30198-nirvana-days:
Cale Young Rice gathers poems in two groups, non-dramatic and more or less dramatic, in a Doubleday volume dated 1909 in Roman numerals. Early lyrics include an invocation, the fairies of God, and a song of the old Venetians. The title poem Nirvana Days joins pieces from off the Irish coast, at Stratford, and before the great Buddha of Kamakura. A vision of Venus and Adonis, a serenata magica, and a Japanese tale of O-Shichi and Moto widen the range.

Dramatic pieces follow, with titles such as Uncrowned, Written in Hell, At the Helm, Dead Love, Mortal Sin, Sea-Mad, and a quatorzain sequence on quest and requital. Rice, author of Yolanda of Cyprus and David, writes in a high, musical style, fond of myth, the sea, and the soul's return. The book suits readers who like late Romantic verse with a wide, wandering eye.
30469-a-tale-of-the-summer-holidays:
G. Mockler presents a children's holiday tale published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1899, built around the four younger Danvers children. Two days after the holidays begin, they receive a note from Drusie. It summons them to a secret gathering the next morning at half seven in the summer house.

Chapters follow a friend in need, Hal finding a friend, disappointed hopes, and a fort in the wilderness. Pictures show Jim scribbling yes on paper, Jumbo washing his face, and a boy throwing a lasso with deadly aim. Mockler writes for young readers who enjoy clubs, codes, and outdoor building, keeping the fun brisk and the friendships warm.
30509-the-railway-builders-a-chronicle-o:
Oscar D. Skelton writes The Railway Builders, a chronicle of overland highways, published in Toronto in 1916. A frontispiece shows a surveyor, often an explorer as well, striking into the wilderness in search of a mountain pass or lower grade, from a drawing by C. W. Jefferys.

Contents move from the coming of the railway and early travel in Canada to the call for the railway and Canadian beginnings. The Grand Trunk era, the Intercolonial, and the Canadian Pacific beginnings follow. Skelton tells how rails crossed a continent, through surveys, companies, and politics, in a clear national chronicle.
3068-washington-square-plays:
Washington Square Plays, volume twenty of the Drama League series, gathers four one-act plays from the Washington Square Players, with an introduction by Walter Prichard Eaton. The Clod by Lewis Beach, Eugenically Speaking by Edward Goodman, Overtones by Alice Gerstenberg, and Helena's Husband by Philip Moeller make the set. Doubleday, Page published the volume in 1925 from copyrights of 1913 to 1916.

A scene from one play has Una ringing a bell, primping at a mirror, and teasing George, a car conductor, for his politeness. The plays show the little-theatre movement's range, from folk drama to psychological comedy. The collection suits readers interested in American experimental theatre of the nineteen teens.
30953-the-boy-scout-and-other-stories-fo:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this collection of stories for boys, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1917, with copyright in 1891, 1903, 1912, 1914, and 1917. Its five stories are The Boy Scout, The Boy Who Cried Wolf, Gallegher, Blood Will Tell, and The Bar Sinister. The frontispiece shows a boy demanding how he is to get ashore.

The title story opens with a rule of the Boy Scouts: every day to do someone a good turn. It applies not because the copy-books say it deserves another indeed, but in spite of that pleasing possibility. Until a true Scout has performed his act of kindness, his day is dark. He is as unhappy as a grown-up who has begun the day without shaving or reading the daily New York Sun. It is a spirited collection of Davis's best boys' tales.
30966-miss-mouse-and-her-boys:
Mrs. Molesworth wrote this children's book, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1897, with pictures by L. Leslie Brooke. It is dedicated to the memory of her brother-in-law, Sir Craven Charles Goring, whose unfailing interest in her work encouraged her through many years. The frontispiece shows a room full of boys, captioned, Oh, what a lot of boys.

Twelve chapters run from What a Lot of Boys and Pat and Pets through Guests at Tea, Wanted: A Sister, Bob, and Ferrets and Fairies. They continue with Nance's Story, Miss Mouse at Home, and The Story of the Lucky Penny. They end with A Great Sacrifice and Out on the Moor. Pictures include a hand-and-pat game down a hill, Nance with stories in her head, and a boy throwing little suns to catch. It is a old-fashioned tale of Miss Mouse and her boys.
3108-nine-short-essays:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote Nine Short Essays on gardens, truthfulness, happiness, literature, and the stage. A Night in the Garden of the Tuileries recalls June 18, 1868, under the Second Empire. It was the longest night Warner ever saw despite short summer nights, spent lounging in Paris gardens and giving none of the balmy nights to sleep. Other essays treat simplicity, the English volunteers, and Nathan Hale. A literature-and-stage essay asks whether the divorce of stage from literature is permanent.

It wonders whether the stage has degenerated or evolved into an independent art, a vinculo or only a mensa et thoro. Warner doubts any recent play carries literary quality. The essays show a thoughtful American man of letters weighing art against popularity.
31278-the-history-of-freedom-and-other-e:
Lord Acton's History of Freedom and Other Essays, edited by John Neville Figgis and Reginald Vere Laurence, was published by Macmillan in 1909, first edition 1907. It gathers seventeen essays reprinted from the Quarterly Review, the English Historical Review, the Nineteenth Century, the Rambler, and other journals. Its title essays trace freedom in antiquity and in Christianity, followed by pieces on Erskine May's democracy in Europe, the massacre of St. Bartholomew, and the Protestant theory of persecution.

Later essays take up political thoughts on the church, Goldwin Smith's Irish history, nationality, Döllinger on the temporal power and his historical work, and Cardinal Wiseman. They go on to conflicts with Rome, the Vatican Council, the Inquisition, the American Commonwealth, and historical philosophy in France. The editors, drawing on Acton's letters to Döllinger and Lady Blennerhasset, present a great historian's liberal mind at full range.
32224-tom-brown-s-school-days:
Tom Brown's School Days, by An Old Boy, was published in New York by Macmillan and Company in 1880. It carries drawings by Arthur Hughes and Sydney Prior Hall, and is the classic Rugby school story. Its frontispiece shows Tom chaired in the quadrangle. The author dedicated the book, without her permission, to Mrs. Arnold of Fox Howe, to whom he owes more than words can repay.

Its contents follow Tom from The Brown Family and The Veast through Sundry Wars and Alliances. The Stage Coach and Rugby and Football lead to After the Match and Settling to the Collar. A War of Independence and A Chapter of Accidents lead into a second part. There the tide turns, a new boy arrives, Arthur makes a friend, and a fight and a fever test the school. Readers get the founding boys' school tale, with football, friendship, and bullying at its heart.
32267-a-century-of-english-essays:
A Century of English Essays, chosen by Ernest Rhys and Lloyd Vaughan for Everyman's Library, number 653, edited by Ernest Rhys, is an anthology of English essayists across a century. Its publishers offer lists of published and projected volumes across travel, science, fiction, theology and philosophy, history, and classical works. They continue through books for young people, essays, oratory, poetry and drama, biography, reference, and romance, in cloth, leather, and library bindings.

The volume's apparatus shows its scholarly care. A small number of printer's errors were corrected by reference to other editions, footnotes moved to just below the referring paragraph, and author lines regularized to appear one line below each essay. Readers get a century of English essays in one Everyman volume, from the essay's classic practitioners, chosen and ordered for general readers.
32334-jacko-and-jumpo-kinkytail-the-funn:
Howard R. Garis's bedtime book tells stories of Jacko and Jumpo Kinkytail, the funny monkey boys, for reading aloud to small children each night. The volume belongs to Garis's long Bed Time Stories series, which also includes Sammie and Susie Littletail, Johnnie and Billie Bushytail, and the Uncle Wiggily books. Each volume in the series holds thirty-one stories, one for each night of the month, with eight coloured illustrations.

Jacko and Jumpo get into the small scrapes and jokes that suit very young listeners, with animal characters, clear morals, and gentle humour. Louis Wisa's pictures accompany the text. Parents and teachers looking for short, nightly read-aloud tales will find this volume in the same friendly pattern as the rest of Garis's animal bedtime books.
32453-molly-brown-s-sophomore-days:
Nell Speed's girls' novel, copyrighted in 1912, follows Molly Brown through her sophomore year at Wellington, where she returns gladly to Queen's Cottage. Molly swings off the bus with her suitcase, running in without ringing the bell, and soon meets juniors and freshmen she knew by sight the year before. Chapters follow Otoyo, a clashing of wits, a tempest in a teapot, an unwilling eavesdropper, and two long-distance calls.

Later the year brings a glee club concert, a Japanese spread, vespers, a great sleet, a skating carnival, and a thaw. Christmas plots, a surprise, and news about how O'Reilly's became Queen's carry Molly toward the turn of the wheel and a garden scene. Speed, author of the Tucker Twins and Carter Girls series, writes warmly about school friendship and growing up.
32496-helen-grant-s-schooldays:
Amanda M. Douglas's Helen Grant's Schooldays, published in Boston in August 1903 with illustrations by Amy Brooks, opens the Helen Grant books. A frontispiece shows Helen telling her dreams to an old apple tree. Chapters begin with Helen herself, an excursion to Hope, air castles with foundations, and the planting of small seeds, in the pattern of Douglas's popular girls' series.

Later volumes in the series follow Helen Grant's friends, Helen at Aldred House, Helen in college, Helen senior, Helen graduate, Helen teacher, and her decision and harvest year. Douglas, author of the Kathie stories and Larry, writes warmly about school, friendship, and growing up. Young readers get a period picture of American girlhood, with dreams, duties, and the slow work of becoming.
3250-how-to-tell-a-story-and-other-essay:
Mark Twain opens this set with his famous essay on telling a story. The humorous story, he claims, is an American development, distinct from the comic story and the witty story. He disclaims the power to tell a story as it ought to be told, but claims to know how it ought to be told, having kept company with expert storytellers for years. The wounded soldier and the golden arm follow as examples.

Mental telegraphy again and the invalid's story round out the volume. Twain's rule is patience: let a story pause, wander, and arrive in its own time. The essays still teach comic timing better than most textbooks. They show a master explaining his craft in the act of practicing it, with jokes that prove each point as he makes it.
32679-geographic-variation-in-red-backed:
E. Lendell Cockrum and Kenneth L. Fitch study red-backed mice of the southern Rocky Mountains in a Kansas Museum paper dated November 15, 1952. Cockrum was drafting a synopsis of North American voles, while Fitch had written a thesis on Wyoming mice, and together they weighed many skins and skulls.

Their work names two subspecies new to science and clarifies two more. The wide-ranging Clethrionomys gapperi galei was typed from Ward, Colorado, at nine thousand five hundred feet. It varies in coat from Wyoming to the Tetons. Northern and southern forms differ in stripe, sides, and skull traits.
32972-round-the-world-in-eighty-days:
Jules Verne's Round the World in Eighty Days appears here in Henry Frith's English translation, transcribed from an 1879 Routledge edition. The story opens in 1872 with Phileas Fogg taking on Passe-partout as his servant, and the wager that follows sends them racing around the globe in eighty days. Trains, steamers, and narrow escapes carry them from London through Asia and America and back again.

Frith's version keeps its own period spellings and turns of phrase, which give this edition a flavor distinct from the better-known Towle translation. Verne's plot, though, needs no help: a cool, exact hero, a loyal servant, and a clock that never stops. It remains one of the great adventure novels, built on timetables, geography, and the thrill of a deadline that cannot be missed.
33040-bye-ways:
Robert Hichens's Bye-Ways, published in New York in 1914, gathers short stories that stray from the main road of his novels. The contents open with The Charmer of Snakes. In it, Renfrew lies awake on a camp bed while jackals whine outside his bell tent and fettered mules stamp on rough ground. The contents then move to A Tribute of Souls, written with Lord Frederick Hamilton, An Echo in Egypt, The Face of the Monk, and The Man Who Intervened.

Later stories include After To-Morrow, A Silent Guardian, A Boudoir Boy, and The Tee-to-Tum, each taking a strange or sidelong turn. Hichens, known for The Garden of Allah and Bella Donna, brings his taste for the exotic and the uncanny to these shorter pieces. The collection suits readers who like a story that begins in a familiar place and quietly leads somewhere stranger.
33055-her-season-in-bath-a-story-of-bygo:
Emma Marshall's Her Season in Bath, published in London in 1889, is a story of bygone days set at the height of the Bath season in 1779. The city then felt the full tide of amusement and pleasure each year, as streets, parades, and terraces filled with visitors seeking fashion, music, and company. Marshall's chapters move from coiffeur and the tide of fashion to music, a vase of Parnassus, and a proposal, before the plot thickens.

Later chapters bring brawls, a challenge, an early morning meeting, and a bitter end, followed by a valley of the shadow and, ten years later, 1790. The novel uses Bath's social world as both setting and judge, where a season's triumphs and blunders follow a young woman for years. It is a gentle historical romance, fond of its period detail and its heroine's fortunes.
33087-discoveries-a-volume-of-essays:
William Butler Yeats's Discoveries gathers his thoughts on poetry, drama, and the life of art. It is a volume of essays printed by the Dun Emer Press at Dundrum in 1907 in only two hundred copies. Its contents run from Prophet, Priest and King and Personality and the Intellectual Essences through The Musician and the Orator and A Banjo Player. They go on to The Looking-glass, The Tree of Life, and The Play of Modern Manners. The essays ask why the blind man in ancient times was made a poet.

Later pieces treat saints, drama, asceticism, and symbolic art, closing with the holy places. Yeats writes from his work with a small theatrical company in the west of Ireland. He argues that drama must root itself in folk life and symbol rather than in drawing-room talk. The book is a key document of the Irish revival.
33213-the-fun-of-cooking-a-story-for-gir:
Caroline French Benton's Fun of Cooking, a story for boys and girls published by the Century Company in 1915 with illustrations by Sarah K. Smith, teaches cooking through story. Its chapters run from the day before Christmas and supper at the house in the woods through Jack's school luncheons and a birthday picnic. They go on to Sunday night supper, Mildred's school party, strawberry time, and camp, before jams and jelly, a Hallowe'en supper, and a time when Mother Blair was sick.

Later chapters bring a doll party, Thanksgiving supper, candy for the fair, and examination day, with an index. Benton, author of A Little Cook Book for a Little Girl, writes for children who want to cook, not merely watch. The book remains a delightful period introduction to the kitchen, where a picnic, a party, and a sick day all teach something useful.
33309-through-the-postern-gate-a-romance:
Florence L. Barclay's Through the Postern Gate, a romance in seven days, was published in 1912. It reached a hundred and forty-sixth thousand printing. Barclay, author of The Rosary, structures the tale by days. Day one brings the story of Little Boy Blue, then Miss Charteris takes control, a boy invades the kitchen, and Christobel signs her name. Guy Chelsea takes control on day five, and Miss Ann has much to say on day six.

The romance's appeal lies in its gentle, domestic magic, where a postern gate opens to love and second chances. Barclay writes with warmth and faith, in a style that made her books bestsellers. For readers who enjoy Edwardian romance, Through the Postern Gate offers a sweet, well-told tale of a week that changes lives.
3331-the-diary-of-samuel-pepys:
Samuel Pepys kept this diary through the 1660s, and it remains the liveliest record of Restoration London. A naval official by day, Pepys wrote at night in shorthand about everything: plays, dinners, quarrels with his wife, office politics, and the great events that broke over the city. Plague in 1665 and the Great Fire in 1666 pass through the entries as personal news.

The diary's charm is its candor. Pepys records his vanities and fears alongside his work, and no entry feels written for posterity. Readers meet Charles the Second's London from the inside: coffee houses, theaters, and streets, all in one man's daily shorthand. It is history as gossip, and gossip that happens to be true.
33389-a-pair-of-schoolgirls-a-story-of-s:
Angela Brazil's Pair of Schoolgirls follows two girls through school days, in the author's familiar, lively style. Brazil, praised for writing schoolgirl tales that other schoolgirls loved, sets the story among classes, games, and friendships, where a pair of heroines learn loyalty, pluck, and fun. The book joins a long shelf of Brazil school stories, from Captain Peggie to The Luckiest Girl in the School.

The tale's charm lies in its true school detail and its warm, comic voice, catching the talk and trials of girls together. Its heroines, by turns bold and kind, carry readers through term-time scrapes. For fans of classic school stories, A Pair of Schoolgirls offers a bright, old-fashioned term with two girls worth knowing.
33421-the-speech-of-monkeys:
R. L. Garner's Speech of Monkeys, in Heinemann's Scientific Handbooks, asks whether monkeys have a true language of their own. Garner, who studied apes at close range, sets out his experiments and his claims for monkey speech, in a book that stirred both wonder and debate. The volume belongs to a series of handbooks that aimed to bring science to general readers.

The book's interest lies in its early, bold attempt to listen to animals as speakers, not just as beasts. Garner's tone is earnest and curious, and his methods, though dated, opened a field still studied today. For readers of animal behavior and science history, it is a fascinating, pioneering work on the border of language and nature.
33521-little-frankie-at-his-plays:
A volume in A. R. Baker's Little Frankie series, this small book follows a young child through his games and playtime lessons. Frankie learns by doing: trying out toys, inventing pastimes, and discovering how to share, take turns, and mind others in play. The simple episodes are written for very young readers, with short scenes and clear morals tucked inside the fun.

As one of several Frankie books covering home, cousins, father, journeys, and school, this volume suits early readers and families reading aloud. Its old-fashioned charm lies in its gentle pace and its belief that play itself teaches patience, kindness, and good manners. The book preserves a nineteenth-century style of children's literature at its most domestic and affectionate.
33668-springtime-and-other-essays:
Sir Francis Darwin gathers essays on nature, books, music, and people in this illustrated 1920 volume. The title essay argues, against governesses who gave each season three months, that spring should take February as well as March, April, and May. That leaves winter a short link of December and January. Darwin writes with a naturalist's eye and a gentle, digressive humor.

Further essays discuss names of characters in fiction, the antiquary Thomas Hearne, recollections, old instruments of music with illustrations of psalteries, lutes, crwths, and recorders, traditional names of English plants. A procession of flowers closes the book. Readers who enjoy reflective, well-informed essays will find Darwin an agreeable companion.
33880-the-land-of-lost-toys:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote this children's book, published in Boston in 1900 with pictures. It opens with an earthquake in the nursery: Sam, a boy with a knack for breaking toys, scalps his twin sister Dot's new doll to roof a wigwam made from bed curtains. Dot, fat, resolute, hasty, and devotedly unselfish, bears the loss with tears and clenched fists.

Later tales follow lost toys and the children who loved them, in Ewing's warm, observant style. She writes for children without talking down to them. The book remains a charming classic of nursery storytelling.
339-old-indian-days:
Charles A. Eastman, Ohiyesa, dedicates these stories of old Indian life to his daughters. Old Indian Days divides into the warrior and the woman, with tales of love, famine, and the white man's errand. The love of Antelope opens on Eagle Scout Butte.

Winona the woman-child, Snana's fawn, and the war maiden follow, with a glossary to close. Eastman, a Santee Sioux physician, writes from inside the culture he describes. His stories honor courage and womanly strength alike. The book preserves a world already passing. Eastman's stories preserve Sioux life as he knew it firsthand.
34005-curious-punishments-of-bygone-days:
Alice Morse Earle wrote this book on old punishments, first published in 1896 and reprinted by Loompanics Unlimited, with pictures by Frank Hazenplug. Earle found her material in old court records, newspapers, diaries, and letters while writing colonial history. A drunkard's cloak fronts the volume.

Chapters run from bilboes, the ducking stool, the stocks, and the pillory through punishments of authors and books. Later chapters treat the whipping-post, the scarlet letter, branks and gags, public penance, military punishments, and branding and maiming. Earle writes with curiosity and a touch of humor. The book gives a vivid look at justice long past.
3499-jo-s-boys:
Louisa May Alcott returns to Plumfield, Jo March's school, in this sequel to Little Men. The chapters follow Jo's boys as young men: Dan, Nat, Demi, Emil, and Josie, with scenes such as Jo's Last Scrape, Dan's Christmas, Nat's New Year, Plays at Plumfield, and Class Day. Marmee's place is now empty, and Meg speaks tenderly of the family that has changed.

Jo, now a teacher and mother figure, watches her pupils face work, love, and loss. Alcott mixes humor with moral lessons, praising kindness, hard work, and courage. The book suits readers who grew up with Little Women and Little Men and want to see Jo's schoolboys become men.
3549-cowley-s-essays:
Abraham Cowley, a seventeenth century English poet, writes essays in this Cassell volume from 1893. An introduction traces Cowley from his father Thomas, a London stationer who died in 1618, through a childhood of early verse. One piece discussed is a sixteen stanza work with songs, first printed in his little Poetical Blossoms at the age of thirteen.

Cowley's essays treat gardens, solitude, work, and the good life with the ease of a man who loved retirement and study. He writes in the plain, personal manner that helped shape the English essay. The volume suits readers who want to meet an early master of the form, before Addison and Steele made it famous.
3667-wolfville-days:
Alfred Henry Lewis writes tales of Wolfville, a fictional cattle and mining town in the Arizona desert, in this collection. Wolfville's cowboys, gamblers, miners, and storekeepers fill stories told in the drawling voice of an old cattleman. The town's saloon, poker games, and street encounters provide the stage for humor, violence, and sudden kindness.

Lewis, a journalist who knew the West, writes with a love for frontier talk and for characters who live by their own code. His stories mix tall tales with sharp observation of a rough society. The book suits readers who enjoy classic western humor and the days when Wolfville stood for the whole wild Southwest.
3706-the-valiant-runaways:
Gertrude Atherton sets this boyhood tale on a great cattle rancho in old California, where two sons of a rich landowner chafe under their father's rule. Roldan, the elder, paces the verandah in a fury at the start, and soon he and his younger brother slip away from home to seek their own fortunes. The rancho world of adobe walls, silver spurs, and grazing herds frames a story about pride, kinship, and the lure of the open road.

Once free, the runaways cross brush country by night, lose their way among owls and bats, and press on toward the nearest town with no shelter in sight. Hunger, fear, and stubborn courage take turns driving them forward. The book suits readers who like frontier adventure told at a brisk pace, with the boys learning that freedom costs more than they had guessed.
3716-mrs-general-talboys:
Anthony Trollope sends a formidable Englishwoman to Rome for the winter of 1859 in this comic tale. Mrs General Talboys claims she comes to drink at the living fountains of classical poetry, though friends suspect a domestic tiff sent her south. Once among the English colony she declaims on the Capitol for Italian unity, praising martyrs' blood and Rome immortal in tones that leave even sympathizers gasping.

The narrator, an Englishman on the spot, admires her fire and winces at her flight, since she soars so high that no plain listener can follow. The tale satirizes grand talk with gentle malice, and Rome itself, with its ruins and revolutions, plays a full part. It is a short study of enthusiasm, and of how a good cause can still make its champion hard to bear.
379-worldly-ways-byways:
Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, gathers forty short essays on manners and society in this 1899 volume. Topics run from charm, dress, and hosts to Paris, Newport, hotels, and the climber's art. Gregory, who knew diplomatic and high society circles, writes as an amused onlooker rather than a reformer.

His pieces poke fun at snobs, dandies, and social exiles while praising ease, wit, and good form. Some essays look back at old Newport or old Paris; others catch new wealth on the move. The book reads as a period guide to how polite folk lived, talked, and judged each other at the century's end.
4006-yesterdays:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's book of poems looks back on days gone by with a moral creed set in verse. Speak no evil, cause no ache, and guard the tongue, she urges, since words are adders when hearts are stung.

The poems move along rough pathways toward the grave, yet they counsel thoughtfulness and bravery rather than gloom. Wilcox writes in plain, musical lines meant to be read aloud and remembered. Readers who like old-fashioned verse with a clear lesson will find short poems for quiet hours, each carrying a small rule for living well.
4035-greek-studies-a-series-of-essays:
Walter Horatio Pater's essays on Greece move from springs and myths to the spirit of Greek art. A fountain of Dirce, haunted by the virgins of Thebes, becomes typical of the coolness of all springs, and the infant god washed there stands for a whole world of myth.

Pater reads Greek story as poetry, finding in rivers, gods, and portents a distant echo of old tumult and wonder. His prose is fine and allusive, meant for readers who know the classics or wish to meet them anew. The essays offer a Victorian critic's loving map of Greece, where myth and art explain each other.
4059-miscellaneous-studies-a-series-of-e:
Walter Pater's miscellaneous essays gather studies of art, poetry, and faith, from Raphael's Disputa to the beauty of pagan philosophy. Pater argues that philosophy and faith, truly apprehended, are as beautiful as Plato thought they must be.

The Disputa, a council of all ages, embodies an idea of truth through art, while other essays weigh antiquarian detail against grace. Pater's technique is perfect in its care, yet beauty stays his ruling test. Readers who like criticism that reads like poetry will enjoy these late essays of a master stylist. Each piece rewards slow reading.
4063-peter-plymley-s-letters-and-selecte:
Sydney Smith's Peter Plymley letters defend Catholic emancipation with wit and plain sense. Smith marvels at servile addresses poured on the throne, and at treating a great question of justice as nothing more than a matter of the monarch's private feelings.

The essays around the letters carry the same voice: a clergyman who argues in clear English, with jokes that cut and logic that holds. Readers who enjoy political satire of the Regency age will find Smith a lively guide to church, state, and tolerance, still readable for his humor and his fairness.
4202-quotations-from-diary-of-samuel-pep:
A book of quotations from Samuel Pepys's diary gathers his most vivid lines, shorn of dates and context. Upon a small temptation, one line admits, he could be false to her, while another frets at his wife's neglect in leaving her scarf.

Waked between four and five by his blackbird, vexed by maids, and over head and ears in getting his house up, Pepys speaks in fragments that still sound whole. The collection suits readers who want Pepys in small bites, for browsing or for finding a line to carry away. It offers the diary's flavor without its full bulk.
436-the-master-key-an-electrical-fairy-t:
L. Frank Baum gives a boy inventor three electrical gifts in this fairy tale of early science. Rob, keen on batteries and motors, meets a Demon of Electricity who grants him devices for travel, food, and force. Rob tests them on cannibal isles, pirate ships, and foreign courts, learning their limits as he goes.

Baum frames the tale as a wonder that may soon prove true, since yesterday's marvels become today's tools. Rob saves a republic, serves a king, and at last gives up his treasures by choice. The book charms as a bright, hopeful story of science as magic for a new century.
4581-the-thrall-of-leif-the-lucky-a-stor:
Ottilie A. Liljencrantz sets this Viking story in the days of Leif the Lucky, when Norse ships reached new western lands. Chapters open where wolves thrive better than lambs, then follow a maid in a silver helmet, a gallant outlaw, a Viking lair, and the ire of a shield-maiden. Leif himself appears as cross-bearer and king's guardsman, while Eric the Red holds his own domain and tales of the unknown west grow bolder.

The hero, a thrall or bondman, must win his way through courts, battles, witch dens, and voyages, with Helga's wooing and a familiar blade in a strange sheath among his trials. The closing chapters reach Vinland the Good, the green western shore the Norse sought. Readers get a stirring historical adventure for young and old, full of ships, swords, loyalty, and the hard road from bondage toward freedom.
4652-escape-and-other-essays:
Arthur Christopher Benson published Escape and Other Essays in 1915. It opens with a Thomas Gray line about people who leave traces of their journey behind them, and advises readers to do so while they can. The contents run from Escape, Literature and Life, and The New Poets. They go on to Walt Whitman, Charm, Sunset, and The House of Pengersick. Then come Villages, Dreams, The Visitant, That Other One, Schooldays, Authorship, Herb Moly and Heartsease, and Behold, This Dreamer Cometh.

Benson's introduction walks down by the river Cam, a stream slighted by lovers of wild scenery. Its chief merit for schoolboys is that it nears a canal in straightness and slow lapse, and so suits their manoeuvres. That quiet manner marks the whole book. Readers get a set of gentle essays on books, places, and moods, by a writer who finds escape in attention to a life close at hand.
4917-the-kellys-and-the-o-kellys:
Anthony Trollope's novel of the Kellys and the O'Kellys opens amid the excitement of Dublin's State Trials in early 1844. O'Connell, his son, repeal newspaper editors, Tom Steele, and Father Tierney stand indicted for conspiracy, and the city follows every proceeding with absorbing interest.

Against that political backdrop, the Kellys and O'Kellys pursue love, money, and family standing in an Ireland stirred by the Repeal movement. Trollope mixes courtroom drama with domestic comedy. Readers get a Victorian Irish novel where public agitation and private ambition keep colliding, told with Trollope's usual patience for character.
4922-bar-20-days:
Clarence E. Mulford's Bar-20 Days sends two tired but happy punchers into a coast town on an errand from their boss Buck, and the pleasures of town life soon overtake the business. Horses stabled and sleeping quarters arranged, the cowboys set out to enjoy what a small city can offer two active young men.

A voice hailing them as cow-wrestlers opens the first of many scrapes, and Mulford keeps the humor rough and good-natured. The stories belong to the Bar-20 ranch world, where loyalty to the outfit matters more than any single adventure. Readers get short, sunny western tales about work, play, and the code of the range.
4953-revolution-and-other-essays:
Jack London's Revolution and Other Essays opens with a letter from Arizona signed Yours for the Revolution, and London answers in kind, counting hundreds of thousands of American socialists behind the greeting. The title essay argues that revolution is not a distant dream but a movement already numbering its adherents.

Other essays follow on the planet's linkage, the house beautiful, gold hunters of the North, the Yellow Peril, and what life means to the author. London writes as a propagandist and a storyteller at once, blunt and vivid. Readers get the socialist London at full stretch, before the novels made his name a household word.
5060-six-short-plays:
John Galsworthy's Six Short Plays gathers one-act and short dramas, opening on a November evening in Keith Darrant's study. The room is large and dark-curtained. A single reading lamp falls on Turkey carpet and books beside an armchair. A deep blue-and-gold coffee service makes an oasis before a log fire. Darrant sleeps there in Turkish slippers and an old velvet coat.

A curtained door opens softly, and Larry Darrant enters, half lost in the curtain, thin and worn. The short form suits Galsworthy's compressed conflicts of family and conscience. Readers get six compact plays, each a single situation pressed to its turning point, ideal for an evening's reading.
5085-characters-of-shakespeare-s-plays:
William Hazlitt's criticism, first published in 1817, takes Shakespeare's plays one by one. It asks what makes each leading figure live on the page and stage. Julius Caesar, Timon, Antony and Cleopatra, Hamlet, Falstaff, Lear, and many others receive short, forceful essays that judge character, motive, and language together.

Hazlitt writes as a reader and theatregoer, not a scholar of sources, and his enthusiasm made the book a model for later Shakespeare criticism. Anyone wanting to read the plays with sharper eyes will find here a lively guide, opinionated and quotable. It treats the characters as people to be understood rather than puzzles to be solved.
5262-curly-and-floppy-twistytail-the-fun:
Howard R. Garis's bedtime book introduces Curly and Floppy Twistytail, the funny piggie boys, in short stories for small children. The tales tell how Curly and Floppy got their names, how Curly helped his mother. He met an elephant, went to school, and was vaccinated. He played with a spinning top, a turtle, chestnuts, and a big apple.

Garis, creator of Uncle Wiggily, writes simple animal stories with gentle lessons and mild mischief. Illustrated by Louis Wisa, the book offers young listeners brief, cheerful episodes, each complete before bedtime, in the familiar world of Garis's animal families.
5264-patty-s-butterfly-days:
Carolyn Wells's Patty's Butterfly Days follows Patty and her friends through a summer of house parties, garden parties, and pageants. Chapters move from Mona's plan and Susan to the rescue, through a dinner party, Aunt Adelaide, Big Bill Farnsworth, a short spin, the worst storm ever. A welcome shelter follows, toward an apple blossom dance and a forced march.

Wells writes light, cheerful stories for girls, full of friendship, flirtation, and small adventures. The book offers a sunny portrait of American girlhood in the early twentieth century, where butterfly days are days of gaiety, freedom, and growing up.
5428-a-defence-of-poetry-and-other-essay:
Percy Bysshe Shelley, the English Romantic poet, argues for the power of poetry and the imagination in this collection of essays. The title essay, A Defence of Poetry, stands beside shorter pieces on love, life, a future state, the punishment of death, metaphysics, morals, and the literature and manners of the Athenians. A piece on Plato's Symposium rounds out the volume.

Shelley opens On Love by asking what love and life even are, then builds toward his larger claim that poets shape how societies perceive the world. Readers get Shelley's philosophy in short form: bold, idealistic, and often lyrical. It suits anyone who wants the poet's mind beyond his verse.
5618-six-plays:
Florence Henrietta Darwin wrote Six Plays, country plays collected in a 1921 Cambridge edition with an introduction by Cecil Sharp and a memoir and portrait of the author. The six plays, sold in paper covers, are Lovers' Tasks, Bushes and Briars, and My Man John. Princess Royal, The Seeds of Love, and The New Year follow, with the middle two bound together.

Sharp introduces them as country plays, rooted in English rural life, song, and custom. Darwin writes for village stages, with folk feeling and plain speech. Readers get a charming set of short plays, suitable for reading aloud or performing, from a writer close to the folk-song revival.
6029-spring-days:
George Moore looks back on Spring Days, a book omitted from his acknowledged works after public and private criticism showed it no mercy. When Henry Vizetelly went to prison for publishing Zola, Walter Scott took over Moore's novels and reprinted all except this one, and Moore himself had lost faith in it.

All the welcome it found was a few contemptuous press paragraphs and an insolent Academy article he never saw, described by a friend in the Strand. Moore recalls dedicating the book to a great reviewer after a night of listening to him quote Greek, English, and Latin classics. The preface frames a novel returning from exile.
6105-their-yesterdays:
Harold Bell Wright dedicates Their Yesterdays to Mrs. Elsbery W. Reynolds, in admiration of a motherhood that gave the race wealth of manhood in her sons and riches of womanhood in her daughter. The book opens at Relay Heights in June 1912, under Pope's lines on a child pleased with a rattle, youth with louder toys, and age with beads and prayer books.

The proem begins simply: there was a man, and it happened that this man went back into his days that were gone, again and again. An illustration shows a woman seeing her home warm with holy love in a fire's glowing heart. Wright follows memory backward, asking what yesterdays still burn in us.
6129-healthful-sports-for-boys:
Alfred Rochefort arranges Healthful Sports for Boys by season, opening in spring with marbles, how played, where and how made, games, terms, and skill. Whip tops, peg tops, kites and their practical uses, hoops, wheels, buzzers, and stilts follow, with fishing, bait, outfit, and care.

Summer brings boating and canoeing with don'ts to observe, small sail boats to make and manage, and swimming in styles, floating, diving, and water games. A chapter on things boys should know covers choosing sides in contests. Rochefort writes a practical, cheerful manual for outdoor play, season by season.
614-across-the-plains-with-other-memorie:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers travel memories and essays in this volume, arranged by a friend from papers written before his South Seas years. Across the Plains recounts an emigrant train from New York to San Francisco, crowded with bewildered folk from four ships. Later pieces treat Fontainebleau, dreams, beggars, and a Christmas sermon.

Stevenson writes with keen, personal prose, even when, as his friend notes, the lights seem turned down by sickness. The volume shows his range: reportage, reverie, and moral talk in one. It serves as a fine companion to his better-known travels, quieter yet just as true.
6141-peck-s-bad-boy-with-the-cowboys:
George W. Peck sends Peck's Bad Boy with the cowboys. The book relates amusing experiences and laughable incidents of a strenuous American boy and his Pa among cowboys and Indians in the Far West. Exciting hunts and adventures mingle with humorous situations and laugh-provoking events, fully illustrated.

The pictures promise Pa kicked by a dog and a grizzly big as a brewery horse. Three cheers for Pa follow, with squaws seeming to worship Pa, and a horse stumbling and throwing Pa over its head. A boy dinosaurus picks up a steer, the pair are captured by Curry's gang, and Pa preaches reform. Peck turns western travel into farce.
6314-biographical-essays:
Thomas De Quincey, author of the Confessions of an English Opium Eater, opens his Biographical Essays with Shakespeare, protagonist on the great arena of modern poetry and glory of the human intellect. Born at Stratford upon Avon in 1564 and baptised on April 25, Shakespeare's birth day rests on tradition, with Malone inferring April 23. De Quincey writes with high praise and close reasoning, weighing fact against legend.

The volume sits in a series whose first book held the Confessions and Suspiria de Profundis, with a third volume of magazine papers promised. De Quincey's essays treat familiarity as a problem, for audiences seeking relaxation often banish Shakespeare, while closets and craving minds return to him. The book is criticism as biography, learned, digressive, and fond of paradox, by a writer who knew opium dreams and English prose alike.
6414-lectures-and-essays:
Thomas Henry Huxley, son of an Ealing schoolmaster and self made intellectualist, stands in his editor's note as the nineteenth century's most noteworthy thinker. His fields were biology, controversy, and pungent criticism of convention. His researches and his attacks on conventional belief probably influenced English science more than any other scientist's work. This 1908 People's Library volume gathers his lectures and essays for a general audience.

Contents run from knowledge of the causes of organic nature, past and present, through Darwin's Origin and hereditary transmission. Man's place in nature follows, with man like apes, fossil remains, and relations to lower animals. Nautilus lives from oldest formations to newest, and Loligo, the modern squid, appears in the lias barely changed. Huxley writes science as argument, clear, combative, and confident that evidence, not authority, must decide.
6570-lectures-and-essays:
Goldwin Smith reprints papers first given as talks or set in journals, at the wish of friends who asked for back numbers they could not find. He leaves politics out on purpose, so the volume stays free of party heat, and he notes that a fuller work on his political thought may come later. Papers on Quebec's conqueror, a king's wirepuller, a captain of industry, and Lincoln's early years lead the set.

Most of the pieces first saw print in Canada, and several came back to Canadian journals, giving the book a clear Canadian cast. Smith writes with the ease of a man used to a lecture hall, keen to inform rather than to stir. Lectures and Essays thus reads as a sampler of a busy mind, kept for friends and now open to all.
6587-king-arthur-s-socks-and-other-villa:
Floyd Dell gathers short plays first staged in Greenwich Village, at the Liberal Club and by the Provincetown Players. The set runs from a five-minute morality play and a comedy on Joseph to a tragic fantasy, a domestic talk piece, and a spoof on Ibsen. King Arthur's Socks, the title comedy, sits among them as a village joke on legend.

Dell calls the plays souvenirs of a witty play-time, now past, and asks for a not-too-solemn memory of it. The pieces are short, talky, and full of the Village spirit of his day. This volume suits readers who like small, clever plays that can be read in an evening or staged with few props.
6666-hello-boys:
Wilcox wrote most of these war verses in France, during seven months spent among American soldiers in camps and hospitals. She says she shaped them in the simplest manner, from close contact with soldiers' minds and hearts, with no thought for critics' rules. Scores of copies were asked for, with autographs, by the men who heard them.

The poems greet the boys by name, cheer them, mourn with them, and send them home in verse. Their plainness is the point: they were made to be spoken aloud in a camp. Hello, Boys is a warm, period book of wartime verse, best read as a voice from the front's waiting rooms.
6909-old-caravan-days:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood sets this tale on the road in 1857, when a caravan starts out with wagons, folk, and children. The contents list a tavern, the Susan house and its cellar, a little old man with a bag, and a great camp meeting where a child's cry sounds at night. Fairy Carrie and the pig headed man, a minstrel, a toll woman, and robbers cross the road in turn.

Jonathan and Thrusty Ellen, Zene's man and woman, and a house with log steps fill the middle chapters with humor and worry. The caravan pushes forward through Sundays on the road, a country Sunday school, and a night picture of home. Catherwood writes a warm road tale of a young America moving west by wagon.
70-what-is-man-and-other-essays:
Mark Twain asks whether human beings are machines shaped by training and habit. What Is Man? and Other Essays gathers the title dialogue with fifteen shorter pieces. An Old Man argues his case to a Young Man, who tests each claim in turn.

The other essays range widely: the death of Joan of Arc, the turning point of Twain's life, and how to make history dates stick. Pieces on Switzerland, Wagner, tobacco, the bicycle, and Shakespeare follow. Twain's humor sharpens a serious question about free will. The collection shows his late mind at its most argumentative.
7150-science-education-essays:
Thomas Huxley's Science and Education essays gather speeches and addresses from more than thirty years, and his preface apologizes for repetitions more needfully than in the first volume. Speeches on one topic, given at intervals to widely distant hearers and readers, could hardly avoid repeating. The oldest piece, on the educational value of the natural history sciences, holds crudities Huxley repudiated when it was first reprinted twenty years before.

Yet much of his later work merely develops propositions from that early, sadly imperfect piece. A recent attempt to disturb the compromise on teaching dogmatic theology, solemnly agreed by the first School Board for London, prompts the fifteenth essay and others. Huxley argues for science in schools, honestly taught and free from sectarian control.
7324-tropic-days:
E. J. Banfield's Tropic Days, from 1918, follows My Tropic Isle with another instalment of sketches from an island off North Queensland, where a few of the original inhabitants kept their uncontaminated ways. Banfield explains that his earlier books aimed at exact, if prosaic, details of island life. Here he again tries to describe types of a crude race in ordinary habit as men and women, not as ethnological specimens, with a tint of imagination to embolden the better truths.

Peace and silence, combined with the large liberties of nature, set the book's mood, in De Quincey's words. Banfield thanks his brother beachcombers in the dedication, and his sketches favour quiet scenes over sensation. The volume reads as a slow, affectionate portrait of tropic life.
7470-castilian-days:
John Hay, who had served Lincoln and would later serve as Secretary of State, knew Spain from his years as a diplomat, and Castilian Days gathers his Spanish essays. The holiday edition of 1903, illustrated from a special visit to Castile by Mr. Pennell, omits a few less descriptive chapters from the original but otherwise reprints the text unchanged. Madrid al fresco opens the book.

Later chapters take up Spanish living and dying, the influence of tradition, tauromachy, or bullfighting, and red-letter days in the Spanish calendar. Hay writes with a diplomat's eye and a poet's ear, admiring Spain without romanticizing it. The essays remain a classic introduction to Castile: its light, its customs, and its stubborn, splendid difference from the rest of Europe.
7554-quotes-and-images-from-the-diary-of:
Samuel Pepys kept his diary through the 1660s, the decade of plague, fire, and Restoration London, and this volume gathers its quotations and images. The reader can copy any short segment, open the diary eBook below, and find the full context. It is a finder and a browser, not a substitute for the diary itself.

The entries catch Pepys in mid-life. There are money and wine needed for a burying, and a good handsome wench kissed. There is a fair salute on horseback in Rochester streets, and a most conceited fellow with not over much in him. A play not very good though much commended, a cat that will be a cat still, and a most tedious sermon all appear. The collection gives Pepys at his frankest, in sentences that still sound alive.
7805-first-plays:
A. A. Milne's First Plays gathers five pieces written in 1916 and 1917, in the order given: Wurzel-Flummery, The Lucky One, The Boy Comes Home, Belinda, and The Red Feathers. Milne says only one touches the war, though the war made the book possible, since soldiering gave a journalist time for a costly gamble.

Playwriting, he jokes, is a luxury like golf, only dearer: articles pay for certain, novels at least get printed, but a play may bring nothing but disillusion. Dedicated to his mother, the volume shows the future Pooh author trying comic stagecraft with wit, warmth, and a soldier's spare hours.
8108-literary-and-social-essays:
George William Curtis collected these literary and social essays, many written for magazines between 1853 and 1891. His subjects include Emerson and Hawthorne from Homes of American Authors, a North American Review study of Hawthorne's works, Rachel the actress. Thackeray in America, Sir Philip Sidney, Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Washington Irving, read at Ashfield and printed by the Grolier Club. The Emerson essay opens with Concord, an hour's ride from Boston.

Curtis writes as a cultivated American man of letters, introducing English and American authors to a general audience. The essays preserve mid-nineteenth-century taste and friendship, since Curtis knew many of his subjects. For readers of American literary history, the volume is a warm, well-informed companion to the age of Emerson and Hawthorne.
8532-andivius-hedulio-adventures-of-a-ro:
Edward Lucas White wrote Andivius Hedulio, adventures of a Roman nobleman in the days of the empire. Maps show the Roman Empire in the second century and the city of Rome under the empire, tracing Hedulio's wanderings. The book, dedicated to the memory of a friend, follows its hero through the empire at its height.

White, a classicist and novelist, writes historical adventure with scholarly care for Roman life, from the city to the provinces. Readers get a tale of travel, intrigue, and Roman manners, grounded in research. The novel suits lovers of Roman fiction who want a hero's travels in a well-built ancient world.
8932-lessons-in-life-a-series-of-familia:
Timothy Titcomb, the pen name of Josiah Gilbert Holland, wrote these familiar essays after his Letters to the Young and Gold Foil won a wide readership. Titcomb states his aim plainly: he does not try to be brilliant or deep. He treats, in a friendly way, the questions that face thoughtful men and women each day.

The essays deal with work, character, money, home, and the conduct of life, in the voice of a wise neighbor rather than a preacher. They sum up the common sense of their age in short, readable pieces. For modern readers they offer a clear window on nineteenth-century American ideals of a good life.
9162-becket-and-other-plays:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate, gathered four plays in this volume: Becket, The Cup, The Falcon, and The Promise of May. Becket, dedicated to the Lord Chancellor, Earl of Selborne, recalls his great predecessor Thomas Becket. Henry the Second, Becket, and bishops such as Foliot and Roger fill its cast.

Tennyson admits the play was not shaped for the modern stage, yet Selborne praised it. The other plays offer shorter trials of love and honor. The volume shows Tennyson's late turn to drama, grave, stately, and rich in historic color.
9255-the-gorgon-s-head-from-a-wonder-boo:
Hawthorne retold the myth of the Gorgon's head for children in A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys, framed by talks on the Tanglewood porch. He held that classical myths could make capital reading for the young, if shaped with freedom. A great freedom was needed, he admits, yet myths stay themselves through change, unlike almost anything else.

So he shaped the old forms anew as fancy dictated, without guilt of sacrilege. Perseus, Medusa, and the winged horse come alive for young readers. The tale remains a beloved gateway to Greek myth, told in Hawthorne's clear, warm voice.
9258-the-miraculous-pitcher-from-a-wonde:
Hawthorne's Miraculous Pitcher, from A Wonder-Book, finds the children in merry May, halfway up a monstrous hill. No longer in the Tanglewood playroom, they climb toward the bald tiptop, a height below Chimborazo or Mont Blanc, yet higher than a thousand ant-hillocks to short childish strides. The hillside frames the tale.

Then comes Baucis and Philemon, whose pitcher never empties for kind guests, and whose humble cottage becomes a temple. Hawthorne retells the myth with warmth for young ears. The story remains a beloved lesson in hospitality, told in his clearest style.
9329-the-widow-o-callaghan-s-boys:
Gulielma Zollinger wrote this children's novel in 1904, in its tenth edition, about the Widow O'Callaghan's boys. Can't I depind on ye, b'ys? asks the frontispiece, as Pat and Mike, Barney, Tommie, and little Jim take on work, geese, roofs, and kitchens. The General makes gravy, Pat markets, and Mike sits on a roof with a knife.

Through mishaps and cheers, the boys learn pluck, loyalty, and care for their mother. Zollinger writes with warm humor and Irish flavor. The book remains a charming family story of a household holding together by grit and love.
9334-the-spectator-volume-1-eighteenth-c:
Henry Morley, professor of English at University College, London, edited this new edition of The Spectator in 1891. It reproduces the original text both as first issued and as corrected by its authors, with introduction, notes, and index. This first of three volumes opens the great eighteenth-century periodical to Victorian readers.

Addison and Steele's essays, on manners, letters, and society, shaped English prose for a century. Morley's notes gloss old customs and allusions. The volume remains a standard scholarly edition, and a fine entry to the Spectator's witty, humane world.
9792-redemption-and-two-other-plays:
Leo Tolstoy wrote Redemption and Two Other Plays, a volume of drama on faith, guilt, and society. Fruits of Culture and Redemption head the contents, with full casts of Russian gentry, gypsies, and servants. Redemption's people include Fedya Protosov, his wife Lisa, and Victor Karenin, with Masha the gypsy girl beside. Officers, doctors, and musicians crowd the stage.

The plays stage moral crisis in drawing rooms and low restaurants, where love, drink, and conscience collide. Tolstoy's drama favors plain truth over stage tricks. A reader gets late Tolstoy on stage, earnest and searching, with Russian life laid bare in speech and act.
a-defence-of-poetry-and-other-essays:
Percy Bysshe Shelley's A Defence of Poetry and Other Essays gathers his prose in one volume. On Love opens the collection by asking what love is, and calling it the bond that connects man with everything that exists. On Life, On a Future State, and On the Punishment of Death follow. Speculations on Metaphysics and on Morals pursue his philosophy.

An essay on Athenian literature, arts, and manners, and his preface to Plato's Symposium, show Shelley the classical scholar. The Defence of Poetry closes the volume, answering Peacock's claim that poetry was obsolete. Poets, Shelley concludes, are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. Written in white heat in 1821, the Defence remained unpublished until 1840. These essays are the prose twin of the lyrics: the same mind arguing that imagination, not reason alone, remakes human life.
a-flock-of-girls-and-boys: Nora Perry gathers a flock of girls and boys in stories for young readers. Its tales include that little Smith girl, the egg boy, Major Molly's Christmas promise, Polly's valentine, and Sibyl's slipper. A boarding school Samaritan, Becky, Ally, and a Thanksgiving guest complete the flock. Perry writes warm stories of school, holiday, and friendship.
across-the-plains-with-other-memories-an:
Robert Louis Stevenson's collection of memories and essays is headed by Across the Plains, his notebook of an emigrant train journey from New York to San Francisco. The contents list twelve pieces. Sidney Colvin's letter at the front explains he chose and arranged papers written before Stevenson left for the South Seas, and notes the last of them were written in gloom and sickness.

After the title essay come The Old Pacific Capital, on Monterey, and Fontainebleau, on the artists' colony in the French forest. An epilogue to An Inland Voyage and two sets of random memories follow. Essays including The Lantern-Bearers, A Chapter on Dreams, Beggars, and A Christmas Sermon round out the volume. Stevenson turns travel notes, boyhood recollection, and moral reflection into one volume, unified by his voice rather than by subject.
andivius-hedulio-adventures-of-a-roman-n: Edward Lucas White tells the adventures of Andivius Hedulio, a Roman nobleman in the days of the empire, dedicated to the memory of Robert Louis Stevenson. The novel follows its hero through Roman streets, courts, and dangers, loving adventure and peril. White's learned romance brings ancient Rome to life with vigour.
angels-and-ministers-and-other-victorian: Laurence Housman gathers angels and ministers and other Victorian plays, opening with the Queen, God bless her, and his favourite flower. The plays revisit Victorian figures and scenes with Housman's gentle irony and pageant style. They offer a playwright's affectionate look back at an age just past. The plays charm most when read aloud.
bar-20-days:
Clarence E. Mulford's Bar-20 Days sends Hopalong Cassidy and Johnny Nelson on a holiday errand. Two tired but happy punchers ride into a coast town and dismount at the best hotel. The marshal makes them hang up their guns with the clerk: this is fence country now. He warns them, smiling, to leave their cash too.

Buck Peters has delegated the mission that brought them from the Bar-20 ranch. Freed of business, the boys sample the town's pleasures as only cowpunchers can. The marshal predicts empty pockets and aching heads within twenty-four hours. Mulford writes the West in dialect, with affection for men smarter than they look. Bar-20 Days is an episodic spree among his Hopalong novels, lighter than the gunfight books and full of bar-room comedy.
becket-and-other-plays:
Alfred Tennyson gathered four plays in this volume, headed by Becket. The laureate dedicated the Becket drama to the Earl of Selborne, the Lord Chancellor of his own day, as a memorial of Selborne's great predecessor. Thomas Becket moves from Chancellor of England to Archbishop of Canterbury in the dramatis personae, with Henry II, Gilbert Foliot, and John of Salisbury ranged around the quarrel of crown and church.

Three shorter plays follow. The Cup sets Roman officers plotting in a conquered province: Antonius signs an order to seize Sinnatus on any trace of treason, hating the Senate's filthy tools even as he obeys. The Falcon turns on a falcon and a vow, and The Promise of May brings the drama home to an English village. Tennyson's late theatre favours verse, conscience, and fate.
biographical-essays:
Biographical Essays, by Thomas De Quincey, gathers the magazine portraits of the author of the Confessions of an English Opium-Eater. De Quincey's volume opens with Shakspeare. He calls the playwright modern poetry's presiding genius. The glory of the human intellect is his other title for him. The essay begins by worrying a small fact with great care. Shakespeare was baptized on the twenty fifth of April, 1564. Tradition makes his birthday the twenty third, the day he also died.

De Quincey builds lives from such grains. His essays treat writers as minds to be entered, not records to be summarized. Digression is the method and the pleasure. This collection belongs to the De Quincey writings series, alongside the Confessions and Suspiria de Profundis.
britannica-1911-bank-holidays:
Bank holidays, in the United Kingdom, are days kept as close holidays in all banks under the Bank Holidays Act of 1871. Before 1834 the Bank of England closed on saints' days and anniversaries some thirty-three days a year. In 1834 those closures were cut to four: Good Friday, 1 May, 1 November, and Christmas Day.

The 1871 act, carried through the Commons by Sir John Lubbock, set Easter Monday, Whit Monday, the first Monday of August, and 26 December as bank holidays in England and Ireland. Ireland added 17 March in 1903. Scotland kept its own list, led by New Year's Day and Christmas Day. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the legal effect: no one must pay or act on such a day, and acting the next day counts as acting in time.
castilian-days:
John Hay's Castilian Days sketches Spain in a holiday edition illustrated after a special visit to Castile by Mr. Pennell. The publishers omitted a few chapters of the original edition, judging them less descriptive and less rich in picturesque material for the illustrator.

Otherwise the text stands unchanged, with contents on Madrid al fresco, Spanish living and dying, tradition in Spanish life, bullfighting, red-letter days, and an hour with the painters. A castle in the air, the city of the Visigoths, the Escorial, a miracle play, and the cradle and grave of Cervantes follow. Readers who love Spain will find Hay's sketches vivid, witty and observant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aliturgical-d:
Aliturgical days are days on which the liturgy, the Eucharistic sacrifice, may not be celebrated. The term, not in any English dictionary, is a convenience label from the modern Greek aleitourgetikos. The idea is far more familiar in the East than in the West. In the Roman Rite only one day is generally recognized as aliturgical: Good Friday. That day the Holy Sacrifice is not offered, and the Mass of the Presanctified contains no prayer of consecration.

In the early centuries, aliturgical days were numerous in both East and West. At first Mass seems to have been offered only on Sundays, the few festivals then recognized, and martyrs' anniversaries, with the bishop officiating. Days of stations, which coincided with the Wednesday and Friday fast, may have gone without the liturgy. Writers such as Tertullian show an opinion that offering the Holy Sacrifice sat ill with a serious fast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-of-da:
Ancient of Days is a name the prophet Daniel gives to God, in chapters seven, verses nine, thirteen, and twenty-two. Daniel sets God's eternal power against the frail life of the empires of the world, and the title carries that contrast in a single phrase.

Christian art drew from these passages its general way of picturing the first person of the Holy Trinity. The name runs in Aramaic as Atiq yomin, in the Greek Septuagint as palaios hemeron, and in the Latin Vulgate as Antiquus dierum, three tongues carrying one image of age without end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bothrys:
Bothrys, now Batroun on the Lebanese coast, was founded by Ithobaal of Tyre, father of Jezebel, near Cape Lithoprosopon. Ancient geographers from Strabo to Hierocles name it, and it served as suffragan of Tyre in Antioch's patriarchate. An earthquake in 551 cracked the cape and opened a large harbor, and Theophanes calls the city Bostrys.

Known Greek bishops number three: Porphyrius in 451, Elias about 512, and Stephen in 553. A tenth-century list still names the see as Petrounion. Today Batroun holds 2,500 people, half Maronite and half Greek, and centers a caza in the Lebanon district. Its Maronite diocese counts 60,000 Catholics, 50 churches, 30 priests, one seminary, 64 schools, and 12 monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-augusti:
A biographical entry presents David-Augustine de Brueys, a French theologian and playwright born at Aix in 1640 and dead at Montpellier in 1723. Raised a Calvinist in a Protestant family, he studied law, then theology with such success that he joined Montpellier's consistory. In 1681 he answered Bossuet's Exposition of Catholic Doctrine.

Soon converted by Bossuet himself, he gave up Protestantism in 1682, becoming a priest after his wife's death. His later works explain his conversion, defend the Mass, outward worship, the Church, and the Eucharist, and treat fanaticism and obedience to rulers. With Palaprat he also wrote comic plays and tragedies, staged with great success and published in 1712, with later editions following.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denys:
A life of Denys van Leeuwen, called the Carthusian, born at Ryckel in 1402 and dead in 1471. A shepherd boy in youth, he studied at Saint-Trond and Zwolle, where rector John Cele shaped his religious leanings. At eighteen he aimed at Saint Bruno's order, but Roermond first refused him as under age, so he studied three years at Cologne.

Admitted in 1423, he lived a hard Carthusian round of Mass, Office, and prayer, often sleeping only three hours a night. Reading filled his cell, from every summa and chronicle to Greek and Arab philosophers and both canon and civil law. Writing filled it too: commentaries on the Psalms from 1434, then the whole Bible and the Fathers, enough to fill twenty-five folio volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ember-days:
Ember Days, from the Latin Quatuor Tempora, or four times, are fast days at the start of each season. Pope Gregory VII fixed them for the whole Church as the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday after 13 December, after Ash Wednesday, after Whitsunday, and after 14 September. Their aims were to thank God for nature's gifts, to teach moderate use of them, and to help the needy.

Their occasion lay in Rome's farm rites, when pagans sought their gods at seeding in December, harvest in June, and vintage in September. The Church, converting pagan peoples, sought to sanctify customs that could serve a good end. Rome at first kept fasts in June, September, and December only, and Gelasius speaks of all four seasons. Saturdays of ember weeks also became days for ordaining priests and deacons. The Eastern Church never adopted them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-druys:
Jean Druys, thirtieth abbot of Parc near Louvain, was born at Cumptich and died in 1635. Schooled at Saint-Trond, Liège, Namur, and Louvain, he joined Parc's Norbertine abbey in 1587, took his licentiate in 1595. He rose through sub-prior and theology teacher to succeed Abbot Loots.

Druys served as vicar-general to Prémontré's abbot-general and sat on Archduke Albert's council and the States of Brabant. He reformed Louvain university as visitor, a task finished in 1617, visited Douai and Héverlé. He rebuilt his own abbey after soldiers' damage, and in 1628 was charged with reshaping his order's statutes to Trent's decrees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurence-hump:
Laurence Humphreys (1571-1591) was an English layman and martyr, born in Hampshire to Protestant parents. A bookish youth, well read in the Bible and religious works, he sought religious debate at eighteen and met Father Stanney, who soon converted him.

Virtuous and kind-hearted, he loved visiting prisoners and the sick, teaching the ignorant, and practising works of mercy, corporal and spiritual. In 1591, seriously ill, in delirium he named Queen Elizabeth harlot and heretic. Overheard by Protestants, he was jailed at Winchester before full recovery. At trial he could not recall the words, yet would not dispute the witnesses and accepted suffering for them. For those words alone he was condemned and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moralities-mo:
Moralities, also called morality plays, grew out of the miracle plays. Together with them they made up most of medieval drama, flourishing in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries across Europe, especially in France. Where a miracle play staged Bible stories, saints' lives and pious legends to teach the faith, a morality staged allegory to shape character.

Its figures were personified abstractions, vices and virtues, qualities of mind and general conceptions, speaking and acting out a moral lesson. Dr. Ward's classic definition puts it that way. Performed outdoors on movable scaffolds with the usual properties, much like miracle plays at first, moralities reached their best-known English form in Everyman. The entry follows their authors, staging and slow decline before the Renaissance stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orkneys:
The Orkneys, islands north of Scotland across the Pentland Firth, hold a Norse-descended, Calvinist, English-speaking people of 30,000 on 375 square miles. Level, rocky, treeless, and partly swampy, they grow barley, oats, potatoes, and beets, and raise 30,000 cattle, 40,000 sheep, and sturdy small horses yearly.

Herring, cod, lobster, seals, whales, and trout feed islanders besides, and down and woven shawls bring export income. Kirkwall, a trading town of 5,000 with a good harbor, serves as capital, and the entry follows Norse earls, Scottish annexation, and the islands' churches. Mining for iron, tin, and silver also goes on successfully across the islands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-plays:
Passion plays grew from medieval religious drama, itself born of church liturgy, not from ancient theatre. Worship was thoroughly dramatic, above all Mass, with its forward action, dialogue of priest, ministers, and choir, and the people's part. Feast Gospels at Christmas, Epiphany, and Easter called for many roles, and poetry and music pressed the great events home to layfolk.

Tenth-century Benedictines of Saint Gall wrote sequences, hymns, litanies, and tropes, musical elaborations of the liturgy, above all the introit, sung antiphonally by choirs. Church drama starts with the Easter introit trope, kept in a Saint Gall manuscript from Tutilo's time, where singers trade the risen Lord's greeting. Later pages trace the plays from church to marketplace, their growth, suppression, and survival at Oberammergau and elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-power-of-the-:
The phrase power of the keys comes from Christ's words to Peter in Matthew 16:19. Its sense opens out in Isaiah 22, where the key of the house of David goes to Eliacim son of Helcias as the mark of full rule in the Kingdom of Juda. By using the phrase, Christ plainly meant to give Peter supreme rule over His Church. Its sole aim is a short history of what church writers have meant by the phrase.

In the Fathers the words crop up often, almost always showing the Church's power to forgive sins. The power to grant or hold back pardon well fits the opening and shutting of heaven's gates. Yet that reading narrows the sense too far, for pardon is but one way church rule is wielded. Augustine's De Doctrina Christi gives a sample of the use.
